questions.question: Determine the convergence of the improper integral below with the best method.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^{3/2} for large x
moves.professor: ln x is a slow creature; x^{3/2} in the denominator breaks its spine. Clean convergence.

moves.name: Integration by parts
moves.professor: Valid, you'll dig up the exact value. But the comparison dagger is faster in open combat.

moves.name: Apply the p-test directly: p=2 > 1, converges
moves.professor: The p-test demands a pure power; ln x poisons that argument. Watch the battlefield.

moves.name: No conclusion; the integral conditionally converges
moves.professor: Conditional convergence doesn't apply to positive integrands. You're parrying shadows.

questions.question: Which test gives the swiftest, definitive verdict for the series below?

moves.name: Ratio Test; limit = 0 < 1
moves.professor: Factorial vs exponential? Ratio Test slices it in a single stroke. Done.

moves.name: Divergence Test; terms go to 0 so it diverges
moves.professor: Going to 0 is the ticket to the game, not the red card. Divergence Test is silent here.

moves.name: Integral Test
moves.professor: You'd have to replace n! with the Gamma function. That's siege equipment for a field skirmish.

moves.name: Limit Comparison with 1/n^2
moves.professor: Limit Comparison: limit is 0, which is inconclusive against a convergent series. Wasted move.

questions.question: Find the limit of the sequence.

moves.name: e, by the definition (1+1/n)^n
moves.professor: The classic limit that births e. Your pattern recognition is razor-sharp.

moves.name: 1, because (n+1)/n → 1 and 1^n = 1
moves.professor: 1^∞ is the oldest trick in the book. The mask hides e. Don't fall for it.

moves.name: Apply L'Hôpital's Rule after taking the log
moves.professor: Logarithm then L'Hôpital gets you there, but that's bringing a ladder when you can just walk through the door.

questions.question: Classify the convergence of the series.

moves.name: Conditionally convergent; AST applies but p=2/3 < 1 so absolute diverges
moves.professor: Alternating signs salvage the slow decay. Conditional convergence, perfect diagnosis.

moves.name: Absolutely convergent; the absolute series is a p-series with p=2/3
moves.professor: p=2/3 < 1 spells divergence for the absolute series. No absolute shield exists.

moves.name: Diverges; terms do not approach 0
moves.professor: 1/n^(2/3) does vanish, slowly but surely. Divergence Test won't fire.

moves.name: Use Ratio Test, limit = 1 so diverges
moves.professor: Ratio Test gives 1—inconclusive. You dodged a trap but left the field without a kill.

questions.question: Determine the best method to evaluate the improper integral.

moves.name: Recognize the p-integral with p=1/2, converges to 4
moves.professor: p=1/2 < 1? Convergent on a finite interval with a singularity at 0. Nailed it.

moves.name: Diverges because the integrand blows up at 0
moves.professor: Blowing up isn't a death sentence. The exponent decides the winner, and it spares this one.

moves.name: Use the substitution u = √x
moves.professor: Gets the job done, cleanly too. But p-test is the faster blade.

questions.question: Identify the flaw in applying the Integral Test to the series below.

moves.name: The function is not decreasing; sin² n oscillates
moves.professor: Integral Test demands a downward slope. sin² n is too chaotic to grant that.

moves.name: It does not apply because the terms are not all positive
moves.professor: sin² n ≥ 0, so the positivity condition holds. Your aim was off, but you didn't crash.

moves.name: The integral ∫ sin² x / x dx does not exist
moves.professor: The integral actually converges, but the test requires monotonicity, which is the real killer.

questions.question: Find the sum of the convergent series.

moves.name: Sum = 3 - 2 = 1
moves.professor: Split it into two geometric series. 2/(1-1/3) = 3, 1/(1-1/2) = 2. Result 1. Perfect.

moves.name: Sum = 2/(1-1/3) + 1/(1-1/2) = 3+2 = 5
moves.professor: Sign error! The second series is subtracted. You marched right into the negative sign.

moves.name: Diverges because 2/3^n diverges
moves.professor: 2/3^n is a geometric series with r=1/3, completely convergent. Missing the forest for the trees.

questions.question: Select the sharpest reasoning for the divergence below.

moves.name: p-integral with p=2 ≥ 1 on (0,1] diverges
moves.professor: At a finite singularity, p≥1 is the lethal zone. Direct hit.

moves.name: The antiderivative -1/x is finite from 0 to 1
moves.professor: -1/x blows to -∞ at x=0. That's infinite area, not finite. Misplayed.

moves.name: Comparison with 1/x shows divergence
moves.professor: Works, but it's a slower path. The p-test is the immediate executioner.

questions.question: Determine the best first move for the series.

moves.name: Ratio Test
moves.professor: Polynomial over exponential? Ratio Test cuts its life short.

moves.name: Root Test yields n^2/n → 1, so inconclusive
moves.professor: Root Test actually gives (n^2)^{1/n} / 2 → 1/2 < 1. It would work, but you misapplied it. Dodge only.

moves.name: Integral Test by integrating x^2/2^x
moves.professor: Integrating x^2/2^x is doable but a slog—wrong weapon for a quick kill.

questions.question: What is the radius of convergence of the power series?

moves.name: Radius = 1, by Ratio Test
moves.professor: Ratio Test gives |x|. The edge is exactly 1. Swift and precise.

moves.name: Radius = ∞, because n grows slowly
moves.professor: Slow growth doesn't grant infinite radius. The geometric core x^n dictates the boundary.

moves.name: Radius = 0
moves.professor: The series plainly converges for |x| < 1. Your radius is too pessimistic.

questions.question: Choose the best comparison to prove convergence of the improper integral.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^2
moves.professor: For huge x, √(x²-9) ~ x, so the integrand is ~ 1/x². The convergent p-test dominates.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x; diverges so the integral diverges
moves.professor: Your target is smaller than 1/x. Being smaller than a divergent giant proves nothing.

moves.name: Trig substitution x = 3 sec θ
moves.professor: Will evaluate it exactly, but you're drawing a two-hander for a shoving match.

questions.question: Why does the series diverge?

moves.name: Divergence Test; limit is e ≠ 0
moves.professor: The terms march towards e, not zero. Divergence Test strikes the fatal blow.

moves.name: Compare with the harmonic series
moves.professor: Each term is near e > 1, much larger than 1/n. The harmonic series isn't the point here.

moves.name: Apply the Integral Test after taking log
moves.professor: Overcomplication. The limit of the terms isn't zero; that's the first and last word.

questions.question: Identify the sum of the telescoping series.

moves.name: Sum = 1/ln 2, because all later terms cancel
moves.professor: Telescope collapse: only the first term survives. 1/ln 2 is the spoils.

moves.name: Sum = 0 because everything cancels
moves.professor: The first term has no predecessor to cancel it. You lost 1/ln 2 in the fray.

moves.name: Diverges because 1/ln n is too large
moves.professor: The telescoping structure forces convergence regardless of individual term size. You dodged but drew the wrong conclusion.

questions.question: Determine the convergence of the series with the optimal test.

moves.name: Diverges by Integral Test; note ln(n^2) = 2 ln n
moves.professor: Simplify the log first; the double logarithm still yields divergence. Integral Test is your friend.

moves.name: Converges because it behaves like 1/(n^2)
moves.professor: 1/(n ln n) is larger than 1/n^2 for most n. Your behavior guess was miles off.

moves.name: Converges by Limit Comparison with 1/n^2
moves.professor: Limit = 0, which against the convergent 1/n^2 is inconclusive. That arrow misses.

questions.question: Which statement is true for a sequence that is bounded and increasing?

moves.name: It converges, by the Monotone Convergence Theorem
moves.professor: Monotone + bounded = convergence. A foundational guarantee.

moves.name: It must be a geometric sequence
moves.professor: Increasing and bounded describes an army, not a single species. Not just geometric.

moves.name: It converges only if it is also Cauchy
moves.professor: True on the real line, but Monotone Convergence is the more direct banner. Overthinking it.

questions.question: What does the series below reveal about its convergence?

moves.name: Converges; bounded by π/(2n^2)
moves.professor: arctan n ≤ π/2, so the series is dominated by a convergent p-series. Flawless.

moves.name: Diverges by Integral Test since ∫ arctan x/(1+x^2) dx diverges
moves.professor: That integral actually converges with a simple u-sub. You didn't check your weapon.

moves.name: Inconclusive; behavior is unknown
moves.professor: The bound is clear as day. Hesitation when the path is lit is a missed opportunity.

questions.question: Evaluate the limit of the sequence.

moves.name: 0; Squeeze Theorem: |sin √n| ≤ 1
moves.professor: Bounded numerator over a growing denominator—Squeeze Theorem crushes it to zero.

moves.name: Limit does not exist because sin √n oscillates
moves.professor: The oscillations shrink to nothing. The denominator silences the noise.

moves.name: Apply L'Hôpital's Rule after continuous extension
moves.professor: Not strictly valid for sequences, but the spirit leads to 0. Squeeze is cleaner.

questions.question: Identify why the improper integral diverges.

moves.name: Split: ∫ 1/x dx diverges, and the constant part also diverges
moves.professor: Split into ∫1/x + ∫1/x^2. The ∫1/x part is the harmonic killer.

moves.name: p-test with p=2, so it converges
moves.professor: The numerator x+1 ruins the pure power. The first term is 1/x, not 1/x^2.

moves.name: Compare with 1/x^2; it converges
moves.professor: Comparisons must respect inequality. (x+1)/x^2 > 1/x, which leads straight to divergence.

questions.question: What is the nature of the series?

moves.name: Conditionally convergent; AST satisfied, absolute series diverges by Comparison to 1/n
moves.professor: Alternating signs and arctan's π/2 bound save it. Absolute ship sinks, conditional sails.

moves.name: Absolutely convergent by comparison with 1/n^2
moves.professor: Absolute terms are near constant/n, not 1/n^2. Divergence is assured.

moves.name: Diverges because cosine would oscillate
moves.professor: There's no cosine. Your eyes slipped. Even if there were, the logic is wrong.

questions.question: Choose the best method to find the sum.

moves.name: Partial fractions into telescoping form
moves.professor: Split and watch the terms cancel. Telescoping series is the cleanest finisher.

moves.name: Use the geometric series formula
moves.professor: No common ratio here. Geometric is the wrong formation for this enemy.

moves.name: Integral Test, then sum the result
moves.professor: You can integrate and partial-fraction the integral, but direct telescoping is faster.

moves.name: Diverges by Limit Comparison with 1/n
moves.professor: The series is actually convergent—terms behave like 1/n^2. Misidentification of the target.
